findings.finding: The plan's edit list for repo_snapshot.py leaves out the code that deletes a donor build that was never published. A donor build hardlinks published files, so deleting it lowers their link counts. That deletion happens in four places: the losing-race rmtree in materialize (line 486), the BaseException cleanup in materialize (line 501) and materialize_tickets (lines 670-671), and the losing-race rmtree of the wrapper inside _publish_ticket_build (line 692). The plan's repo_snapshot.py bullet puts only 'the donor attempt … the publish rename and the exclusive_size increment' in the single lock hold, and says nothing about whether these deletions run inside it. If any of them runs after the lock is released, an evictor can measure the donor entry while the leftover tmp hardlinks still raise its files' link counts. It then subtracts nothing for those files, and they are later freed with nothing subtracted: the same kind of drift this ticket fixes.

findings.finding: The plan holds the store-wide lock across 'the donor attempt', which in the code is the whole materialize_via_donor call. That call includes donor-candidate search: `_tree_paths` (git ls-tree) for the target, then up to 8 candidates, each with its own ls-tree and `git diff`. Then come read-tree and checkout-index. Every one is a git subprocess bounded only by _GIT_TIMEOUT=300s. The Cost section lists only 'the hardlinks, read-tree, and a checkout-index of the changed paths', so it understates the hold. All evictions, all publishes (including full-build publishes, which also need the lock), and startup_sweep can stall behind one slow donor search. checkout-index may also lazy-fetch over the network, because _ensure_blobs_present is best-effort. Only _link_tree_paths through publish (or discard) changes link counts, so candidate selection and diffing can safely run before the lock is taken. A donor evicted in between makes os.link fail, and _link_tree_paths already treats that as fall back to the next candidate.
findings.location: Approach — repo_snapshot.py bullet ('It runs the donor attempt (hardlinks plus delta rewrite) ... in a single lock hold') and Cost paragraph
scenarios: A ticket tip advances every ~26s (ADR 0005). Each populate holds the store-wide lock through up to 17 git subprocesses, so code-entry publishes and GC evictions queue behind it.
A slow or hung git diff on a large repo holds the lock for up to 300 s per call, blocking the janitor's eviction under disk pressure.
findings.suggested_fix: Refactor delta_tree into a planning step that returns (donor_entry, link_paths, deletes, writes) without the lock, and an apply step that runs _link_tree_paths + _apply_delta under the lock. On a link failure, release the lock and try the next planned candidate or fall back to a full build.

findings.finding: The invariant 'outside the store's accounting lock, a file's link count counts only links from published entries' is not maintained on three non-success paths. First, a donor build that fails partway leaves hardlinks to published files in its tmp/ tree; so does a donor build whose publish rename loses the race. The plan only specifies the success path ('when the donor build succeeds, the publish rename and the exclusive_size increment in a single lock hold') and never says these tmp trees are removed before the lock is released. Second, a process killed mid-donor-build leaves tmp/ hardlinks that persist across restarts. startup_sweep is not specified to purge tmp/ under the lock before its walk. Third, the plan does not say whether donor selection happens inside the lock. If it does not, an evictor can delete the chosen donor while the populater waits for the lock.

findings.finding: Several cleanup steps change link counts outside the accounting lock, so the plan's invariant does not hold in failure and startup cases. (a) The plan holds the lock in startup_sweep only 'across its authoritative walk and reset'. sweep_tmp and drain_trash run before that, without the lock. start_background_janitor runs startup_sweep in a daemon thread while the server is already populating, so sweep_tmp can rmtree an in-flight donor build that holds links. (b) _gc_pass calls drain_trash before any eviction, without the lock. (c) _evict's `shutil.rmtree(dest, ignore_errors=True)` can fail partway and silently leave trash links. A later eviction of a published entry sharing those inodes then measures nlink 2 and frees 0, and the eventual drain_trash removes the bytes uncounted, so the total overcounts. The plan's claim 'so the trash copy's links are gone before the next measurement' assumes rmtree always succeeds.

scenarios: The server starts, and a gate populates a ticket entry by donor build while the janitor thread's startup_sweep runs sweep_tmp, deleting the tmp build and its donor hardlinks outside the lock.

janitor.py:308-309: `startup_sweep` also calls `sweep_tmp(root)` and `drain_trash(root)` before the walk. The plan only says the lock spans "its authoritative walk and reset".
findings.finding: The invariant's list of lock-holding sites misses `drain_trash` as called from `_gc_pass` (janitor.py:457). The plan only puts `_evict` and `startup_sweep` under the lock. But `_gc_pass` runs `drain_trash(root)` without the accounting lock before every reclamation pass. `drain_trash` runs `shutil.rmtree` on trash stragglers left by an interrupted eviction. A straggler can still share inodes with a published entry: B hardlinked from A, then A was renamed to trash before its rmtree. Removing it drops a published file's `st_nlink` outside the lock, which breaks the plan's own rule.
findings.location: Approach — `src/rebar/_snapshot/janitor.py` bullet ("`_evict` holds the lock … `startup_sweep` holds it across its authoritative walk and reset")
scenarios: janitor.py:457 `_gc_pass` → `drain_trash`: a straggler's link to an inode shared with published entry B is removed while a populater measures B under the lock. If the populater sees two links and adds 0, then after the drain the file sits only in B and is counted nowhere. This is the same undercount the plan fixes, by a path the plan leaves unguarded.
janitor.py:308-309 `startup_sweep` → `sweep_tmp`/`drain_trash`: these run before the locked walk. If the lock hold starts after them, these unlinks also happen outside the invariant.
findings.suggested_fix: In the janitor.py bullet, state that `_gc_pass` runs `drain_trash` under `cache.accounting_lock`, and that `startup_sweep` takes the lock before `sweep_tmp`/`drain_trash` and holds it through the walk and reset. Derive the full list of link-removing sites with `find_referencing_symbols` on `drain_trash`, `sweep_tmp` and `_evict`, plus a string grep for `rmtree` and `unlink` under src/rebar/_snapshot.

No statement of lock acquisition order anywhere in the Approach
findings.finding: The plan adds a store-wide accounting lock held across long operations, but it states no lock ordering relative to the existing single-flight mechanism or any per-entry/refcount locks that populate and evict already take. One wrong nesting is enough to deadlock: a populater holds the single-flight lock and waits on the accounting lock, while the evictor holds the accounting lock and waits on an entry lock.
findings.location: Approach — cache.py / janitor.py / repo_snapshot.py bullets
scenarios: A populate takes the per-SHA single-flight lock, then accounting_lock. _evict takes accounting_lock, then checks or takes a per-entry lock or refcount lock. The two deadlock.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State (and verify) that interprocess_lock excludes threads in the same process as well as other processes, and list every call made under the held lock that must use the held-lock add_bytes variant.
evidence: "returns the existing interprocess_lock on <root>/locks/bytes.total.lock"
Testing: "runs the other actor in a second thread"
findings.finding: The fix and the tests both assume that interprocess_lock excludes threads within one process as well as separate processes. The plan does not state this. If the lock is built on POSIX fcntl record locks, which are owned per process, two threads would both 'acquire' it. The tests run actors in threads, and in-process concurrent populates would not be serialized. Reentrancy is also load-bearing: anything called while the lock is held must use the held-lock variant, or a flock on a fresh fd deadlocks. The plan does not enumerate which calls need that.
findings.location: Approach — cache.py bullet; Testing
scenarios: Under fcntl-based locking, the second thread in test 1 is not blocked. The race happens even with the fix, and the cause is hard to diagnose.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that interprocess_lock excludes threads within a process (or add an in-process lock layer), and list every lock-taking call made from inside the new held sections (startup_sweep reset, anything _evict or the donor build calls) with a held-lock variant for each.
evidence: "add `accounting_lock(root)`, which returns the existing `interprocess_lock` on `<root>/locks/bytes.total.lock`"
"`add_bytes` takes it and delegates to a held-lock variant that callers already holding the lock use" — only add_bytes is given a held variant
"`startup_sweep` holds it across its authoritative walk and reset" — the reset write path is not given a held variant
Testing: "runs the other actor in a second thread ... is waiting on `cache.accounting_lock`"
findings.finding: The plan's correctness and its tests depend on two properties of the existing `interprocess_lock` that it never states. (a) It must exclude threads within one process as well as separate processes. The new tests run both actors as threads in one process and expect the second to block. POSIX fcntl/lockf record locks do not exclude threads of the same process. (b) The held sections must not call anything that re-acquires the lock. The plan gives add_bytes a held-lock variant, but startup_sweep's 'reset' and any lock-taking helpers called from _evict or the donor build get no such treatment. If the lock is not reentrant, those calls deadlock.
findings.location: Approach — cache.py bullet (accounting_lock); janitor.py bullet (startup_sweep reset); Testing
scenarios: If interprocess_lock is fcntl-based with no in-process threading lock, two populate/evict threads in one process enter the critical section together. The race persists in threaded callers, and the interleaving tests never observe a wait.
If startup_sweep's reset calls a lock-taking setter while the sweep already holds the lock, startup deadlocks.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend the Cost section to cover publish waits behind rmtree, the startup walk and git subprocesses, and specify a timeout or bounded wait (or a log/metric for long lock holds and waits) for the accounting lock while git subprocesses run under it.
evidence: "Cost: donor-path populates serialize with each other and with eviction for the length of a delta build (the hardlinks, `read-tree`, and a `checkout-index` of the changed paths). Full materializations still build concurrently."
"`_evict` holds the lock from `exclusive_size` through the rename to trash, the `rmtree`, and the decrement"
"`startup_sweep` holds it across its authoritative walk and reset"
Absence: no timeout, no stale-holder handling, no instrumentation of lock waits
findings.finding: The plan holds one store-wide interprocess lock across external git subprocesses (`read-tree`, `checkout-index`), across `rmtree` of an evicted entry, and across startup_sweep's full-store walk. It gives no timeout or bounded wait, and no logging of lock hold or wait time. The Cost section mentions only donor-vs-donor and donor-vs-eviction serialization, and claims 'Full materializations still build concurrently'. But full materializations, and every other accounting call, must take the same lock to publish. They therefore queue behind any slow git subprocess, large rmtree or startup walk. A hung git process would block every populate and eviction in every process sharing the store, with no visibility.
findings.location: Approach — repo_snapshot.py and janitor.py bullets; 'Cost' paragraph
scenarios: `git checkout-index` stalls on a loaded host. Every concurrent snapshot publish and eviction across all processes blocks indefinitely.
A large entry's rmtree under the lock delays all publishes. Under `make verify` load this lengthens test runs and may trip timeouts elsewhere.
